hero.body: Type your question the way you would say it. We find relevant sections in the published sources, explain them in plain language and show you the original wording beside them.

preview.label: Example answer to the question: can police search my phone?
preview.question: Can police search my phone?
preview.answer: Your phone calls and messages are private under Section 37. Police can only override that under a law made for reasons like public safety or preventing crime, as Section 45 allows.
preview.sectionTitle: Section 37 · Right to private and family life
preview.edition: This is the 1999 Constitution as published in 2004. Later amendments aren't included yet.

problem.title: The Constitution is written for lawyers. Your question is not.
problem.body: It runs to 320 sections and 7 schedules of formal legal English. The words you would search for are rarely the words it uses.
problem.pdfTitle: You search for “phone”. Nothing comes up.
problem.pdfBody: The section you need talks about “telephone conversations and telegraphic communications”, and the limits on it sit eight sections later.
problem.appTitle: You ask “can police search my phone?”
problem.appBody: Section 37 comes first, Section 45 comes with it for the limits, and the answer explains both in two sentences.

tagline: The Constitution belongs to every Nigerian.

benefits.title: Answers you can understand and check

items.title: Ask in your own words
items.body: Everyday words, Pidgin or a half remembered section number. “Section thirty something about privacy” still finds Section 37.

items.title: The answer comes first
items.body: You get a direct reply to what you asked, then what it means for you and where the limits are. No legal jargon to decode.

items.title: The official wording, every time
items.body: Every answer shows the exact text of the sections it relies on, with citations taken from the published source.

items.title: Keep what you find
items.body: Copy an answer with its citations, save sections for later, or open the page in the printed source to check it yourself.

faq.title: Before you ask
faq.body: The short version: it is free, it is independent, and it always shows you the source.

items.a: No. constitution.ng explains published Nigerian legal sources and shows you the exact section. If you are facing a court case, an arrest or a dispute, speak to a lawyer or the Legal Aid Council. Bring the sections you found here with you.
Yes. Asking questions, finding sections and reading the published source edition are free. There is no paid plan.
No. You can ask and read as a guest. Create an account only if you want your conversations to follow you to another device.

It is the 1999 Constitution as published in 2004. Amendments passed after that are not included yet, so a section may have changed since. Every answer tells you this so you can check before you rely on it.

The law picker lists the laws in the selected published release. A law under review is not available there. Each provision identifies its source edition. Acts labelled as enacted may have been amended; check the original source and later changes before relying on them.
Yes. Ask the way you would say it, in English or Pidgin, and we will find the section. You can also switch the site to Pidgin, Yorùbá, Hausa or Igbo. The official wording is always the English text.

items.q: How do you choose the section?
items.a: Your question is matched against published sections, using both the words you typed and what you mean. Citations come from the text itself, never guessed, and every answer lists the sections it used so you can read them yourself.
Yes. Copy any answer with its citations, or save the sections you need. Quote the official wording, not the explanation, when accuracy matters.
No. constitution.ng is independent. It is not published by, or connected to, the National Assembly or any government body.
